name: PIQA: Physical Interaction Question Answering
description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding systems. The dataset consists of multiple choice question answering pairs where a model must choose the most appropriate solution to a physical goal from two options. It contains over 16,000 training QA pairs with an additional 2K and 3K held out for development and testing respectively. The dataset is inspired by instructables.com and focuses on everyday situations with a preference for atypical solutions.
creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)
citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI 2020.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) annotators who were prompted with links to instructables.com. Annotators were asked to glance at the instructions of an instructable and construct two component tasks, articulating a physical goal and a valid solution, plus a 'trick' (an invalid but plausible-sounding solution). Annotators were seeded with instructables drawn from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop. Two examples were drawn per instructable. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. This often meant that correct examples were removed that required expert level knowledge of a domain (e.g., special woodworking terminology) which should not fall under the umbrella of 'commonsense.'
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructions from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for doing everything from cooking to car repair. Annotators used these as inspiration to construct goal-solution pairs.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm, which performs systematic data bias reduction by discarding instances whose given feature representations are collectively highly indicative of the target label. In practice, 5,000 examples from the original dataset were used to fine-tune BERT-Large and compute embeddings of all remaining instances. AFLite uses an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets of the data to determine whether pre-computed embeddings are strong indicators of the correct answer option.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: AFLite algorithm was applied to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples. Goals were tokenized by Spacy. The GPT BPE tokenizer was used for solution tokenization. The longest 1% of the data was removed for analysis. During model experiments, examples were truncated at 150 tokens, affecting 1% of the data. Train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were provided with a prompt derived from instructables.com and asked to: (1) provide a physical goal, (2) provide a valid solution, and (3) provide a 'trick' - a solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. A qualification HIT was run prior to the main annotation stage where annotators had to successfully identify (>80%) well-formed and underspecified (goal, solution) pairs. Validation HITs were also run after the main annotation stage. Users with low agreement were de-qualified. An interface with a diff button was provided to highlight where solutions differ.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Examples with low agreement during validation were removed from the data. Human performance was calculated by majority vote. Annotators chosen for human performance evaluation achieved 90% on the qualification HIT. Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr according to both self-reporting on turkerview.com and timing calculations.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite algorithm using BERT-Large embeddings; Spacy for tokenization; GPT BPE tokenizer
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance AI systems' understanding of physical commonsense knowledge, which is critical for day-to-day human life including problem solving. The authors hypothesize that modeling physical commonsense knowledge is a major challenge on the road to true AI-completeness, including robots that interact with the world and understand natural language.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT. Reporting bias was identified as a challenge during data collection, where annotators tended toward prototypical solutions and common tools. AFLite was applied to reduce annotation artifacts. The distribution of referenced objects was flattened by prompting annotators with instructables links.
rai:dataLimitations: Large pretrained models struggle with the dataset (~77% accuracy vs 95% human accuracy). The dataset focuses on English only. Models pretrained on large web crawls may eventually surpass human performance by finding large sources of in-domain data, but this does not address the underlying limitation of learning physical knowledge from language alone. The authors note that knowledge should ideally be learned from interaction with the world.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluation of physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding models. The dataset is intended for testing/evaluation purposes to measure the gap between model and human performance on physical commonsense tasks. It can also be used as a diagnostic tool to probe the physical knowledge captured by deep pretrained language models.
